hook.title: Your AI writes a bug. The framework catches it.
hook.lede: Your assistant has read more React than anything else, so its first Pyreon draft comes back React-shaped and compiles fine. Pyreon ships the tools it checks its work against: an MCP server with 24 tools, the compiler's live/static verdict in your editor, `pyreon check` and generated `llms.txt`.

stats.label: MCP tools: get_api, validate, diagnose, explain_reactivity and more
stats.condition: tool list checked against the docs page by a CI step

stats.label: network calls from the MCP server: no model inside, deterministic answers

sections.title: A plausible draft, caught before you see it.
sections.text: Two bugs that are not syntax errors: a signal "written" by calling it, and a React `key` on a list. The button never counts, and the list never gets the `by` it needs. The assistant passes the draft to the MCP `validate` tool first.

blocks.label: The draft
validate (real output, trimmed)
blocks.code:
Found 2 issues:

1. **signal-write-as-call** (line 9)
   `count(value)` does NOT write the signal — `signal()` is the read-only callable
   surface and ignores its arguments. Use `count.set(value)` to assign or
   `count.update((prev) => …)` to derive from the previous value. …
   Current: `count(count() + 1)`
   Fix: `count.set(count() + 1)`
   Auto-fixable: yes

2. **for-with-key** (line 10)
   `key` on <For> is reserved by JSX for VNode reconciliation and is extracted
   before the prop reaches the runtime. In Pyreon, use `by` for list identity.
   Current: `key={(i) => i.id}`
   Fix: `by={(i) => i.id}`
   Auto-fixable: yes

sections.caption: Each finding carries its code, line, the offending text, the fix and an auto-fixable flag, so the assistant applies the fix instead of guessing.

sections.title: Five tools, one source of truth.
sections.text: The API answers come from the same per-package manifests that generate the docs and `llms.txt`, and CI fails when they drift.

items.title: MCP server
items.text: `@pyreon/mcp` speaks JSON-RPC over stdio and never modifies your files. `validate` runs three detector families (React habits, Pyreon misuse, native-build hazards), including `props-destructured`, `signal-write-as-call`, `for-missing-by` and `array-map-jsx`. Configs are documented for Claude Code, Cursor and Windsurf.

items.title: Reactivity Lens
items.text: `pyreon-lint --lsp` draws `live`, `live·prop`, `live·attr`, `static` and `hoisted` next to each JSX expression. Watch for `static` where you expected `live`: it reviews whatever your assistant just pasted.

items.title: `pyreon check`
items.text: The terminal twin of `validate`. It scans git-changed files (or a folder), prints each finding with its fix, applies the auto-fixable ones with `--fix`, and exits non-zero, so it fits a pre-commit hook or a CI step.

items.title: `@pyreon/lint`
items.text: 133 rules in 25 categories, with an LSP server, watch mode and an AST cache. Silence one line with `// pyreon-lint-ignore <rule>`.

items.title: `llms.txt`
items.text: `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` sit at the root of the repository, generated from the manifests. An assistant that cannot speak MCP reads them directly.

blocks.label: Your terminal
blocks.code:
pyreon check            # git-changed .ts/.tsx files
pyreon check src/       # a directory
pyreon check --fix      # apply the auto-fixable rewrites

sections.title: Or let the scaffold wire it.

items.title: Pick your assistants
items.text: `--ai` takes `mcp`, `claude`, `cursor`, `copilot` and `agents`. The default, `mcp,claude`, writes `.mcp.json` and a `CLAUDE.md`; `copilot` writes `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.

items.title: Approve the server
items.text: Open the app in your editor, approve the Pyreon MCP server, and ask for a feature. Watch what your assistant checks.

sections.text: The server makes no network calls and runs no long scans at startup.

items.q: Do the detectors know my types?
items.a: No. They read syntax, not types, so a signal used in arithmetic without being called (`count + 1`) slips past them. TypeScript flags that one, so keep `tsc` in the loop.

items.q: Does this make the model smarter?
items.a: No. It gives the model something to check its work against. Whether it calls the tools depends on the client and the prompt, which is why the scaffolds write the instructions for you.

items.q: Is the Lens on the VS Code Marketplace?
items.a: Not yet. VS Code uses an extension from the repo; other editors register `pyreon-lint --lsp` by hand.

items.label: Reactivity Lens
items.text: The hints, and how to enable them.

end.title: We cannot change what a model was trained on. We can change what it checks its work against.
